title: The Point
summary: The Point is a Shinnecock Reservation marshland remembered through community use for fishing, hunting, gathering, and teaching across generations. The listing speaks from local Shinnecock landscape knowledge and does not direct readers to sensitive areas.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: For generations, Shinnecock families have utilized the rich marshlands of The Point to harvest wild resources like snow geese and huckleberries and to teach traditional hunting skills to their youth. Preserving these active communal harvesting practices demonstrates that Indigenous ecological knowledge is not a relic of the past, but a living, practical tradition that continues to sustain Native communities today.
history_content:
Resources remembered by Shinnecock elders

The Shinnecock Environmental Department’s 2014 catalogue names The Point in its resource accounts. These sections preserve the places named in that 2014 community record. Present-day access, abundance, and harvesting rules may differ.

Geese

Geese supplied food and feathers, including fans used around fires and in clothing. Elders’ accounts of hunting at The Point emphasize care around nests and rules followed by outsiders hunting on Shinnecock land in the 1980s. The catalogue lists Canada geese, brant, and snow geese. PDF pp. 12–13.

Shadbush / serviceberry

The catalogue links shadbush flowering with the end of frost and preparations for the spring shad run. It remembers the fruit as food and an ingredient in pemmican. The plant is a seasonal sign connecting land, water, and work. PDF p. 17.

Huckleberries

Huckleberries appear as an important part of Shinnecock food life, gathered with other berries and used in pies. The catalogue names dwarf and blue huckleberries and connects berry knowledge with woodland edges. PDF p. 18.

Coral honeysuckle

The catalogue treats coral honeysuckle and introduced Japanese honeysuckle as separate plants. It records aromatic and medicinal traditions and describes how Japanese honeysuckle became part of local practice. PDF p. 22.

Explore all resources and places in the catalogue.

Shinnecock Environmental Department, Natural Resources Identified by Shinnecock Elders, April 4, 2014, PDF pp. 12, 13, 17, 18, 22. Page numbers count the cover as PDF page 1.
